newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Now coffee hits $3 per pound.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Now coffee hits $3 per pound.

text.p: A spectacular rally in coffee prices accelerated on Thursday to lift New York futures above $3 per pound for the first time in 20 years.
London prices for the less-prized robusta beans couldn't match a gain of 150 percent since January on the arabica types that are traded in New York.
Even so, they put on almost 15 percent in just a few frenzied hours of buying to rise above $2,500 per tonne. This was double where they began 1997.
Forecasts for cool winter weather in Brazil, the biggest exporter, do not so far signal a damaging frost.
But supply is already tight from Latin America. Stocks are at the lowest in two decades. So the market is in a panic as Brazil's frost scare season begins.
"There are no more fundamentals to talk about," said one New York trader. "Everyone's just buying it. Who is going to sell it?"
The benchmark New York July arabica contract hit $3.07 per pound, up more than 11 cents from Wednesday.

Latest data in Tokyo meanwhile showed a jump of 13.5 percent in April coffee imports by Japan as roasters there scrambled to buy coffee in the tight world market. Retailers continue to levy increases in the shops in the United States and Europe.

"This is an historic moment - but also a worrying one. These prices could start to hit consumption as housewives may start buying smaller quantities," says Jorge Esteve, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters Association.
The view among traders in Brazil is that hitting the $3 mark may bring some profit-taking to the futures arena, but that prices could pick up again afterwards on concern about the risk of a frost.
After September, however, if there is a frost-free winter, they are likely to slip towards $2 and lower, as supplies from Central America come in.
Other commodity markets could not match the excitement in coffee on Thursday.
The price of gold was itself stubbornly unmoved amid the turmoil over what Germany does with its bullion reserves.
It fixed in London at $343.90 an ounce which was up from $342.80 on Wednesday.

But dealers were unsure how much that reflected news late Wednesday that the Bundesbank rejected a government plan to revalue German reserves, to use the paper profit to plug gaps in the 1997 budget and bring Germany within criteria for European Monetary Union (EMU).

Andy Smith, bullion analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland, said the German row could be positive for gold, against a backdrop of present fears that European central banks may sell metal to meet EMU rules.
EMU might be postponed, or go ahead on the basis that balance sheets would be massaged. Either way "the need for gold sales is reduced..." Smith said.
Palladium hit a new record high official price on Thursday at $196 an ounce, on Russian supply concerns in what continues to be a very tight market.
